stem: A 73-year-old man with terminal lung cancer cannot breathe without a ventilator. He is alert, understands his prognosis, and has asked on several days to have the ventilator removed because of constant suffering. A psychiatric evaluation shows no depression. His three children insist that ventilation continue.
oneliner: 73M + terminal lung cancer + ventilator dependent + alert and repeatedly asks to stop + no depression + children object → best action?

options.A: Keep the ventilator on until the children consent to stopping
options.B: Request a court order before the ventilator is stopped
options.C: Keep the ventilator but decline any new treatments
options.D: Remove the ventilator and treat his distress
options.E: Let the hospital ethics committee decide whether to stop

whyNot.A: The patient has capacity, so his choice prevails and **family consent is not required**
whyNot.B: A court is needed when **capacity or wishes are in doubt**; he is **competent and consistent**
whyNot.C: Ignores his explicit request; **withholding and withdrawing are ethically equivalent**, and this would not end the suffering he describes
whyNot.E: A committee advises when an **incapacitated** patient's wishes are unclear; he can decide for himself

answer: Remove the ventilator and treat his distress
why: A **competent adult** may refuse any treatment, including life support. **Withdrawal is ethically and legally equivalent to withholding**, and relatives cannot override a patient with capacity. Provide comfort care (opioids, sedatives) as the ventilator is removed.

idea.rule: A capable patient's informed refusal overrides the wishes of the family.
also: An adult Jehovah's Witness with capacity may refuse a transfusion
Artificial nutrition and hydration may be withdrawn like any other treatment
Surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity
Comfort medication that may hasten death is acceptable if relief is the intent (double effect)

stem: A 52-year-old man with metastatic small cell lung cancer has just entered hospice care for severe bone pain, rated 9 on a 10-point scale. He has no history of substance use, is alert, and breathes comfortably at 14 per minute. A short-acting oral opioid was started yesterday and his pain is only partly relieved.
oneliner: 52M + metastatic small cell lung cancer in hospice + bone pain 9/10 + no substance use + alert, respirations 14 + pain partly relieved on new opioid → best action?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding his pain medication?

options.A: Cap the dose to avoid causing addiction
options.B: Raise the dose until his pain is controlled
options.C: Keep the dose minimal to watch for side effects
options.D: Keep the supply away from him to prevent overdose
options.E: Replace the opioid with an NSAID alone

whyNot.A: In **end-of-life care** addiction is not a limit, and he has **no history of substance use**
whyNot.C: A **pain score of 9** only partly relieved needs more drug, not less
whyNot.D: He is **alert** with no stated wish to harm himself; withholding access leaves the pain uncontrolled
whyNot.E: **Severe cancer bone pain** needs an opioid; an NSAID alone is inadequate

answer: Raise the dose until his pain is controlled
why: In hospice the goal is **comfort**, so the opioid is **titrated until the pain is controlled**. Fear of **addiction or respiratory depression** should not limit dosing when the intent is to relieve suffering; his respirations are normal.

idea.rule: At the end of life, adequate symptom relief outweighs concerns about addiction.
also: Pure opioid agonists have no ceiling dose and are titrated to effect
Add a bowel regimen, since opioids cause constipation
Relief is the intent, and respiratory depression is an accepted risk (double effect)
NSAIDs and radiation are useful adjuncts for painful bone metastases

stem: A 50-year-old man who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day and runs five days a week has just been told that his lung biopsy shows non-small cell carcinoma. He stares at the physician and says, "I can't believe it. I eat well, I work out, I take care of myself."
oneliner: 50M + smoker who exercises + new non-small cell lung cancer + says "I take care of myself" → best response?
ask: What should the physician say next?

options.A: Don't worry, I promise everything will work out well.
options.B: Healthy eating and exercise do not prevent lung cancer.
options.C: Smoking a pack a day is the biggest risk factor for this.
options.D: Whatever your habits are, we need to begin treatment soon.
options.E: This must be hard to accept when you feel so healthy.

whyNot.A: False reassurance: nobody can promise the outcome of a **new cancer diagnosis**
whyNot.B: Gives blunt facts and ignores his **emotional disbelief**
whyNot.C: Blames him while he is **already distressed** by the news
whyNot.D: Rushes to treatment before he has **absorbed the diagnosis**

answer: "This must be hard to accept when you feel so healthy."
why: A patient who reacts to bad news with **disbelief** needs his feelings **acknowledged first**. An empathic statement that names the emotion is better than reassurance, blame, further facts or an immediate treatment plan.

idea.rule: When a patient reacts emotionally to bad news, acknowledge the emotion before giving facts or plans.
also: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy
Use open-ended questions and allow silence
Do not give false reassurance or false hope
Ask what the patient already understands before explaining

stem: A 31-year-old man who has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 12 years comes for a routine visit. He has no cough or dyspnea. When asked about quitting, he says he knows smoking is bad for him and will quit sometime, but he does not feel ready to try now.
oneliner: 31M + smokes 1 pack/day for 12 years + no respiratory symptoms + knows the harm + not ready to quit now → next step?
ask: What is the best next step with him today?

options.A: Ask him to list the pros and cons of quitting
options.B: Explain the long-term lung and heart risks of smoking
options.D: Advise a nicotine patch to begin today

whyNot.B: He **already acknowledges the harm**; more facts will not move someone who is not ready
whyNot.C: Drug therapy suits patients **ready to quit**; he is not
whyNot.D: Replacement therapy also needs a patient **ready to try**
whyNot.E: He has **no respiratory symptoms**, and testing does nothing about his readiness

answer: Ask him to list the pros and cons of quitting
why: He is in the **contemplation stage**: aware of the harm but **not ready**. **Motivational interviewing**, asking him to weigh the pros and cons in his own words, builds readiness. Drugs and a quit date wait until he is prepared.

idea.rule: Match the intervention to the stage of change.
also: Precontemplation: raise awareness without pressure
Contemplation: weigh pros and cons (motivational interviewing)
Preparation: set a quit date and offer pharmacotherapy
Action and maintenance: support and prevent relapse

stem: A 51-year-old man is evaluated for lung transplantation because of end-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. He has an IQ of 68, major depression controlled on medication for six years, and obsessive-compulsive disorder treated with therapy. He and his wife often argue. He says he gave up cigarettes years ago, but his wife reports he still smokes a pack daily.
oneliner: 51M + end-stage pulmonary fibrosis + IQ 68 + treated depression + treated OCD + marital arguments + wife says he still smokes → strongest contraindication?
ask: Which of the following is the strongest contraindication to transplantation?

whyNot.A: Stressful but not a bar; he still has a **spouse involved in his care**
whyNot.B: **Controlled** psychiatric illness does not exclude him
whyNot.D: Not a contraindication by itself if he can follow a regimen with support
whyNot.E: **Treated** and stable, so it is not a bar

why: Candidates must avoid what damaged the organ and must **adhere to treatment**. **Active smoking** after a fibrotic lung disease is the strongest psychosocial contraindication; **controlled depression, OCD, mild intellectual disability and marital strain** are not absolute bars.

idea.rule: Active substance use is the key psychosocial barrier to transplantation, while controlled psychiatric illness is not.
also: Alcohol-related liver disease needs documented abstinence before liver transplant
Poor adherence to treatment is a relative contraindication
Active malignancy or uncontrolled infection also bars transplant
Stable, treated psychiatric disease does not exclude candidates

stem: A 34-year-old woman has asthma that remains uncontrolled on her inhalers. She is invited to join a study of a new inhaled drug. The study will randomize 1,800 patients with asthma at 90 centers to the new drug, an existing controller or placebo, with neither patients nor investigators told the assignments. Dose and short-term safety were settled in earlier studies, and the results will be submitted for approval.
oneliner: 34F + uncontrolled asthma + study of 1,800 patients randomized double-blind to new drug, controller or placebo + dose already set + results go to approval → which phase?
ask: In which phase of drug development is this study?

whyNot.A: Microdosing in a few people to check drug handling; it **does not test efficacy** or involve 1,800 patients
whyNot.B: Small group, mostly healthy volunteers, for **safety and dosing**, which are already settled here
whyNot.C: Hundreds of patients at most, for **efficacy and dose-finding**; this study is much larger and heads for approval
whyNot.E: Happens **after approval**; this drug is still awaiting it

why: A **large, randomized, double-blind** trial in patients with the disease, comparing a new drug with placebo or standard therapy before approval, is **phase 3**.

idea.rule: Phase 3 is the large randomized trial that confirms benefit before approval.
also: Phase 0: microdosing in a few volunteers to check pharmacokinetics
Phase 1: small group of healthy volunteers, safety and dose
Phase 2: patients, efficacy and dose-finding in the hundreds
Phase 4: post-marketing surveillance, which finds rare adverse events

stem: In a 12-week trial, 96 adults with asthma received a new inhaled drug and 98 received placebo. The mean daily symptom score was 2.6 in the drug group and 2.9 in the placebo group (higher is worse), a difference of 0.3. The p-value for the difference is 0.035.
oneliner: Trial: 96 on new inhaled drug vs 98 on placebo + mean symptom score 2.6 vs 2.9 + p = 0.035 → what does p mean?
ask: Which of the following is the correct interpretation of the p-value?

options.A: 3.5% of treated patients did better than the average placebo patient
options.B: The drug worked in 3.5% of the patients who received it in this trial
options.C: There is a 96.5% probability that the drug truly works in this population
options.D: The probability that the drug has no effect is 3.5% in this trial
options.E: With no true effect, a gap at least this large occurs 3.5% of the time

whyNot.A: The p-value concerns the **gap between group means**, not a share of individual patients
whyNot.B: Also reads p as a share of patients; it is a **probability about the data**, not a response rate
whyNot.C: p is **not the probability that the drug works**; it assumes no effect and asks how unusual the data are
whyNot.D: p is **not the probability that the null hypothesis is true**; it is conditional on the null

answer: If the drug has no effect, a difference at least this large would occur 3.5% of the time by chance
why: The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference **at least as large as 0.3 if the null hypothesis were true** (no drug effect). It is not the chance that the null is true, the chance the drug works, or a proportion of patients.

idea.rule: p-value = probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
also: Significant at alpha 0.05 means p < 0.05
A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05
Type I error rate equals alpha, chosen before the study
A small p-value says nothing about effect size or clinical importance

stem: Researchers reviewed the records of 640 men admitted to a single university hospital over five years. Men with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease had a higher risk of myocardial infarction than men without it (odds ratio 3.1, 95% CI 1.8 to 5.2).
oneliner: Single-hospital record review of 640 admitted men + COPD vs no COPD + MI odds ratio 3.1 → results generalize to whom?
ask: To which population can these results most reasonably be generalized?

options.C: Men with COPD living at home
options.D: All patients with COPD, in or out of hospital
options.E: Hospitalized men with a myocardial infarction

whyNot.C: The sample was drawn only from **admitted** patients, who tend to be sicker
whyNot.D: Includes **women and outpatients**, neither of whom were studied
whyNot.E: The groups were defined by **COPD status**, not by infarction

why: External validity extends only to people **like the study sample**. The sample was **men admitted to one hospital**, so the result applies to **hospitalized men with COPD**, not to women, outpatients or all patients with COPD.

idea.rule: Results apply only to people like the study sample (external validity).
also: Internal validity is the absence of bias within the study itself
Trial volunteers may differ from real-world patients
Strict exclusion criteria narrow the population a result applies to
A tertiary-center sample may be sicker than community patients

stem: Researchers randomly assigned 240 children aged 4 to 11 years with a viral upper respiratory infection, recruited from emergency departments, to receive dextromethorphan syrup or no treatment. Parents knew which group their child was in. Two nights later, parents rated cough severity on a validated 5-point scale, and children given the syrup scored lower (p = 0.002).
oneliner: Randomized trial of 240 children with viral URI + dextromethorphan vs nothing + parents knew group + parent-rated validated cough scale + p = 0.002 → greatest threat to validity?
ask: Which of the following is the greatest threat to the validity of this study's conclusion?

options.A: Parents who rate the outcome knew the assignment
options.B: Too few participants to detect a difference
options.C: A p-value too close to the significance cutoff
options.D: Recruitment of children from emergency departments only
options.E: Use of a rating scale rather than a laboratory test

whyNot.B: A **significant result (p = 0.002)** in 240 children shows adequate power
whyNot.D: Affects **generalizability**, not whether the comparison itself is biased
whyNot.E: The scale is **validated**; subjectivity matters here only because **raters were unblinded**

answer: Parents who rate the outcome knew the assignment (no blinding)
why: With **no placebo and unblinded parents scoring a subjective outcome**, placebo effect and observer bias can produce the difference. Lack of blinding is the main threat to **internal validity**.

idea.rule: Blinding protects a subjective outcome from placebo effect and observer bias.
also: A placebo control equalizes expectations between groups
Double-blind means neither participants nor assessors know the assignment
Randomization addresses selection bias and confounding, not observer bias
A single-center sample limits external, not internal, validity

stem: A cohort study followed coal miners and non-miners for the development of chronic bronchitis. Over one year, new cases occurred at a rate of 31.5 per 1000 miners and 9.0 per 1000 non-miners.
oneliner: Cohort: chronic bronchitis incidence 31.5 per 1000 in miners vs 9.0 per 1000 in non-miners → attributable risk?
ask: Which calculation gives the attributable (excess) risk of chronic bronchitis from mining, per 1000?

whyNot.A: The ratio of the two incidences is the **relative risk**, not the excess
whyNot.B: Adding the two rates has **no epidemiologic meaning**
whyNot.D: This is the **attributable risk percent** (71.4%), a proportion, not a rate per 1000
whyNot.E: The inverse of the relative risk; it is **not a standard measure** of excess

why: **Attributable risk = incidence in the exposed minus incidence in the unexposed** = 31.5 − 9.0 = **22.5 per 1000** per year. The ratio (3.5) is the relative risk, and dividing the excess by the exposed rate gives the attributable risk percent.

idea.rule: Attributable risk is the absolute difference in incidence; relative risk is the ratio.
also: Relative risk here = 31.5 ÷ 9.0 = 3.5
Attributable risk percent = (RR − 1) ÷ RR = 71.4%
Number needed to harm = 1 ÷ 0.0225 = 44.4, rounded up to 45 miners for one extra case per year
Population attributable risk uses the whole population's incidence minus the unexposed incidence

stem: A review of lung cancer deaths in men who smoke reports that about 71% of those deaths would not have occurred if the men had never smoked. The authors want to name this measure.
oneliner: Report: 71% of lung cancer deaths in male smokers would not have occurred without smoking → which measure?
ask: Which of the following measures does this value represent?

whyNot.A: The chance that a positive **test** truly means disease; no test is described
whyNot.B: A ratio of rates, a number such as 3.5, not a **share of deaths**
whyNot.C: The proportion of a population with a disease at one time, not the **share due to an exposure**
whyNot.E: New cases per population per time, not the **proportion explained by smoking**

why: The **share of disease in the exposed that is due to the exposure** is the **attributable risk percent**: (incidence exposed − incidence unexposed) ÷ incidence exposed, or (RR − 1) ÷ RR.

idea.rule: Attributable risk percent = the proportion of cases in the exposed that is due to the exposure.
also: AR% = (RR − 1) ÷ RR
A relative risk of 3.5 gives an AR% of about 71%
Attributable risk (absolute) is the difference in incidences
Population attributable fraction also depends on how common the exposure is
